passage: At the community centre's after-school room, the boys picking football teams called every name but Chaitanya's. "Don't care," he said, and dropped onto the beanbag with the old tablet, thumbs flying through a racing game. Vandana, who ran the centre, watched his jaw tighten each time the ball thumped outside. She didn't ask him to talk. She sat on the next beanbag and started sorting coloured pencils. "Being left out stinks sometimes," she said to nobody in particular. "If you ever feel like telling me about it, I'm here till six." Chaitanya kept racing. At quarter to six, without looking up, he said, "They always pick me last." Vandana nodded. "Thanks for telling me."

qa.q: What game did Chaitanya play on the tablet?
qa.a: He played a racing game.

qa.q: How can you tell Chaitanya felt more hurt than he let on?
qa.a: His jaw tightened each time the ball thumped outside, and later he admitted they always pick him last.

qa.q: What choice did Vandana make, and why did it work?
qa.a: She sat nearby and left the door open to talk without pushing, so he could open up in his own time.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel when Chaitanya finally speaks at quarter to six?
qa.a: She is probably quietly glad that her patience let him share something painful.

grounding: A boy claims not to care about being left out and buries himself in a game, and an adult invites his feelings without pressure.

passage: My little sister Neelam, nine, found out today that the whole class got invited to Pooja's party except her. At dinner she said, "Who cares, parties are boring," and went straight back to her cartoons on Papa's phone, volume up. She didn't laugh at the funny bits. I don't know what's going on in her head. Mummy didn't push. She just said, "If it bothers you later, you can tell me. Or not. Either is fine." Later I heard Neelam in Mummy's room, talking in a small voice. I couldn't hear what she said. I'm Kalyani, by the way. I left my last chocolate on her pillow.

qa.q: Whose party was Neelam not invited to?
qa.a: She was not invited to Pooja's party.

qa.q: What does Neelam not laughing at the funny bits suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was hurt about the party, even though she said she didn't care.

qa.q: How did Mummy's words help Neelam?
qa.a: She invited Neelam to talk without pressure, which let Neelam come to her later in her own time.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Neelam's "Who cares, parties are boring"?
qa.a: She seems to sense hurt behind it, so she offers a gentle, open invitation instead of arguing.

grounding: An older sibling watches a nine-year-old claim not to care about being left out and hide in cartoons, while their mother invites her feelings without pressure.

passage: Everyone in Year 5 in Leeds had got an invitation to Felix's birthday except Emeka. "Don't care," he told his dad at the school gate, hitching his bag higher. "Parties are boring." At home he went straight to the tablet and played the racing game for two hours, jaw tight, jabbing at the screen. His father didn't take the tablet away or push. He brought two bowls of jollof rice, sat on the arm of the sofa and said, "If you ever feel like talking about Felix's party, I'm around. No rush." Emeka kept racing. But at bedtime he said, very quietly, "It was only me who didn't get one."

qa.q: How long did Emeka play the racing game?
qa.a: For two hours.

qa.q: What does Emeka's tight jaw while playing suggest?
qa.a: That he was hurt and left out, even though he said he didn't care.

qa.q: Which choice of his father's worked, and why?
qa.a: Offering to talk with no pressure, because it let Emeka share the hurt at bedtime in his own time.

qa.q: How might Emeka's father feel hearing the quiet sentence at bedtime?
qa.a: He may feel sad for Emeka and also glad the invitation to talk was finally taken up.

grounding: Shows a child who claims not to care about being left out and buries it in a game, while an adult invites feelings without pressure.

passage: At the district swimming club, the relay list went up on the board, and Charu's name wasn't on it. The other girls crowded round, squealing. Charu shrugged. "Relays are stupid anyway." She sat on the changing-room bench, earphones in, playing a puzzle game on her phone with fierce attention. Coach Ganga saw that she didn't look up for twenty minutes. She didn't lecture. She sat at the other end of the bench, sorting kickboards. "I'm here till six," she said. "If you want to talk about the list, or not, either's fine." Charu kept tapping. On her way out, she stopped. "Can I train with the relay girls anyway?"

qa.q: What was Charu playing on her phone?
qa.a: A puzzle game.

qa.q: What might Charu be feeling behind "Relays are stupid anyway"?
qa.a: She is probably disappointed and hurt at being left off the list, hiding it behind the game.

qa.q: How did Coach Ganga invite Charu's feelings without pressure?
qa.a: By sitting nearby, busy with kickboards, and saying she was available to talk or not until six.

qa.q: How might the other girls see Charu's shrug?
qa.a: They might think she really doesn't care, missing that she was hurt.

grounding: Illustrates a child brushing off being left out by burying it in a phone game, while an adult stays available without pushing.

passage:
Saturday: The colony boys picked teams and left Ojas out. "Whatever. I'd rather play on the computer," he said, and spent the afternoon building a fortress in his game, door shut. His elder brother Dhruv knocked once. "Snacks, if you want." No answer.
The next Wednesday: While they brushed their teeth, Dhruv mentioned, "I got dropped from the team in Class 5. It stung for ages." Ojas said nothing, but didn't leave.
The Sunday after: Ojas came and sat on Dhruv's bed. "They said I'm too slow," he muttered. Dhruv listened and didn't try to fix it. Later they went down together to bowl at the wall.

qa.q: What did Ojas build in his game on Saturday?
qa.a: A fortress.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling behind "Whatever"?
qa.a: He was hurt and ashamed about being left out, hiding it in the game behind a shut door.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped Ojas open up?
qa.a: He offered snacks without pushing, shared his own story of being dropped and later just listened.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel when Ojas finally sits on his bed?
qa.a: Dhruv may feel relieved and trusted, since his patient invitations worked.

grounding: Shows over days a child who hides being left out in a game and slowly opens up when invited without pressure.

passage:
Preeti, beta, you say you don't care that they didn't invite you. I said that too, once. Listen to your Noor Nani.
When I was ten, the girls in my class made a skipping group and never asked me. I told everyone, "Who cares? I like carrom better," and played carrom alone for hours. At home, tears were for babies.
Then a new teacher came, Miss D'Souza. She never said, "Tell me your problems." She just sat down at my carrom board one lunch and played, and came back the next week, and the next.
One day she said, "If you ever want to talk, I'm here. If not, we'll just play." For a month I said nothing. Then one afternoon I told her about the skipping group, and I cried on the board.

qa.q: What game did young Noor play alone?
qa.a: Carrom.

qa.q: How did young Noor feel about being left out, beneath what she said?
qa.a: She said "Who cares?" but was really hurt and lonely, which came out when she finally cried telling Miss D'Souza.

qa.q: What choice did Miss D'Souza make that let young Noor open up?
qa.a: She kept showing up to play without asking questions, then offered to listen with no pressure, leaving the choice to Noor.

qa.q: How might Miss D'Souza have felt waiting a month for Noor to talk?
qa.a: She probably needed patience and hope, choosing to trust that steady games would help rather than pushing.

grounding: Shows a grandmother recalling how, as a child who claimed not to care about being left out, a teacher's pressure-free invitations let her feelings come out.
